Every time you look at the night sky, you're looking backwards. The light hitting your retina left the star years—sometimes millennia—ago. Betelgeuse might have already exploded, and we wouldn't know for centuries. The universe, it turns out, only offers us archives, never the present tense.

This is true on Earth too, at smaller scales. The sunlight warming your face is eight minutes old. When you look at the moon, you see it as it was a second ago. Even a conversation is an exchange of pasts: sound takes milliseconds to travel, light takes longer, neurons take longer still. We are all, permanently, slightly out of sync.

I find this strangely comforting rather than melancholy. It means nothing is ever truly lost. The light from dead stars keeps traveling, carrying their image outward like a message in a bottle. Somewhere, theoretically, an observer positioned just right could watch all of Earth's history unfold in order—dinosaurs, cathedrals, first steps on the moon—simply by standing far enough away and pointing a sufficiently absurd telescope.

We tend to think of the past as gone. Physics suggests it's more accurate to say the past is elsewhere, still in transit, radiating outward at the only speed the universe permits. Memory is just biology's humble attempt to do what light does naturally: hold onto what has happened, carry it forward, let it be seen again. And sometimes, standing somewhere dark, you catch a few of those travelers arriving—messages that left home before you existed, arriving just in time for you.
